question: Who asked Jesus for the best seats in heaven?
summary: In Mark 10:35-37, James and John themselves come to Jesus and ask for the seats at his right and left in his glory. In Matthew 20:20-21, the mother of Zebedee's sons does the asking on their behalf. Same Markan pericope, same request, same place in the narrative — but the petitioner has changed from the disciples to their mother.

reconcile.connective: Clarke harmonizes the two accounts by casting the mother as spokesperson while Jesus, aware of the true petitioners, answers James and John directly.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells (Skeptic's Annotated Bible) presses the plain reading: Mark's direct petitioners and Matthew's substitute petitioner cannot both be the literal historical scene.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/best_seats.html

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: In the 'Historical Discrepancies' chapter (p. 347), Haley treats this exact pairing directly, applying the same principle he uses for the centurion of Matt 8:5/Luke 7:8 ('qui facit per alium, facit per se' -- what one does through another, one does oneself): Zebedee's wife makes the request for her sons in Matthew 20:20, while they make it for themselves in Mark 10:35.

link.title: Mark 10:35—Who came to talk with Jesus, the mother of James and John or James and John?
link.note: live apologetic treatment posing this exact question, cross-referencing the companion Matt 20:20 discussion (Geisler & Howe, When Critics Ask)

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The request here mentioned, Matthew says, Mat 20:20, was made by Salome their mother; the two places may be easily reconciled thus: - The mother introduced them, and made the request as if from herself; Jesus knowing whence it had come, immediately addressed himself to James and John, who were standing by; and the mother is no farther concerned in the business.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke states explicitly that Mark's 'James and John come unto him' and Matthew's mother-as-petitioner describe the same event: the mother spoke, and Jesus answered the sons directly.
